## 2. Layout techniques

raw_comment:
I notice that the minimum daily temperatures between June and August have increased for every city depicted in these graphs when compared to the 1960s. I also take note that the percentage of days considered “abnormally hot” is always significantly higher than days considered “abnormally cold” for these cities. For example, in Phoenix, less than 1% of nights have been abnormally cold yet 49% of the days were abnormally hot, and Chicago has seen less than 1% abnormally cold days and 61% abnormally hot ones.
I wonder what has caused these increases in temperature, especially considering that these are minimum temperatures being recorded. I wonder if this something that we as humans can avoid or reverse,  and if these such increases are avoidable, what practices should be abandoned because they contribute to an overall spike in minimum summer night temperature.
The findings of these graphs relate to my community and me because we are the ones living through these times and trends. Additionally, hotter temperatures contribute to detrimental health issues, such as heat stroke, heat exhaustion, and sunburn, while also raising the need for energy for air conditioning, possibly resulting in money loss.
An appropriate headline for this graph is: “Don’t Blame It on Me, Blame it on the Night: Why do Minimum Nighttime Summer Temperatures Seem to be Increasing?”

- **Faceted density/distribution chart** (small multiples of overlaid smoothed distributions).
- Each panel shows temperature distributions for a city, with shaded regions highlighting unusually cold and unusually hot nights.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: separate panels for different cities.
- **Layering/overplotting**: multiple filled distribution shapes are overlaid within each panel.
- **Reference lines**: vertical dotted lines mark thresholds for abnormal cold/hot.
- **Text annotations**: percentages and labels are placed directly on panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City (Phoenix, Las Vegas, San Francisco, New Orleans, Houston, Chicago, Atlanta, New York (JFK), Washington) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Summer minimum temperature (°F) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Frequency / distribution of nights | Quantitative | Height/shape of filled density area (y-position/area) |
| Time period: 1960s | Temporal | Fill color (light gray) and direct label |
| Time period: 2020s | Temporal | Fill color (orange/pink shaded distribution) and direct label |
| Abnormally cold nights | Categorical/derived | Blue shaded tail area to the left of cold threshold; annotation text |
| Abnormally hot nights | Categorical/derived | Pink/red shaded tail area to the right of hot threshold; annotation text |
| Cold threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Hot threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Percent of nights abnormally cold | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |
| Percent of nights abnormally hot | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |

- **Faceted density/distribution chart** (small multiples of overlaid smoothed distributions).
- Each panel shows temperature distributions for a city, with shaded regions highlighting unusually cold and unusually hot nights.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: separate panels for different cities.
- **Layering/overplotting**: multiple filled distribution shapes are overlaid within each panel.
- **Reference lines**: vertical dotted lines mark thresholds for abnormal cold/hot.
- **Text annotations**: percentages and labels are placed directly on panels.

## 3. Data variables

|---|---|---|

| Summer minimum temperature (°F) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Frequency / distribution of nights | Quantitative | Height/shape of filled density area (y-position/area) |
| Time period: 1960s | Temporal | Fill color (light gray) and direct label |
| Time period: 2020s | Temporal | Fill color (orange/pink shaded distribution) and direct label |
| Abnormally cold nights | Categorical/derived | Blue shaded tail area to the left of cold threshold; annotation text |
| Abnormally hot nights | Categorical/derived | Pink/red shaded tail area to the right of hot threshold; annotation text |
| Cold threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Hot threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |

raw_comment:
I noticed that New Orleans has the biggest change as 64% of the nights were abnormally hot. The least place with abnormally hot nights is New York which is at an only whopping 17% which is significantly less than New Orleans.

I wonder why these cities were specifically picked. Is it because they can get accurate recordings or is it maybe a point of interest as perhaps these places may have shown a great amount of environmental changes throughout the years.

This relates to my community because it brings some awareness into me and my community and how we can try to prevent our cities from getting abnormally hot at night. Hawaii is already a pretty clean place when it comes to factories and gasses being produced here but the location (Hawaii) itself is just hot.

In the graph they show some cities temperature changes throughout 2020 and record how abnormally hot it has been in the night. A catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea is “Desertification of the world.”

- **Faceted density/distribution chart** (small multiples of overlaid smoothed distributions).
- Each panel shows temperature distributions for a city, with shaded regions highlighting unusually cold and unusually hot nights.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: separate panels for different cities.
- **Layering/overplotting**: multiple filled distribution shapes are overlaid within each panel.
- **Reference lines**: vertical dotted lines mark thresholds for abnormal cold/hot.
- **Text annotations**: percentages and labels are placed directly on panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City (Phoenix, Las Vegas, San Francisco, New Orleans, Houston, Chicago, Atlanta, New York (JFK), Washington) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Summer minimum temperature (°F) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Frequency / distribution of nights | Quantitative | Height/shape of filled density area (y-position/area) |
| Time period: 1960s | Temporal | Fill color (light gray) and direct label |
| Time period: 2020s | Temporal | Fill color (orange/pink shaded distribution) and direct label |
| Abnormally cold nights | Categorical/derived | Blue shaded tail area to the left of cold threshold; annotation text |
| Abnormally hot nights | Categorical/derived | Pink/red shaded tail area to the right of hot threshold; annotation text |
| Cold threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Hot threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Percent of nights abnormally cold | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |
| Percent of nights abnormally hot | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |

- **Faceted density/distribution chart** (small multiples of overlaid smoothed distributions).
- Each panel shows temperature distributions for a city, with shaded regions highlighting unusually cold and unusually hot nights.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: separate panels for different cities.
- **Layering/overplotting**: multiple filled distribution shapes are overlaid within each panel.
- **Reference lines**: vertical dotted lines mark thresholds for abnormal cold/hot.
- **Text annotations**: percentages and labels are placed directly on panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City (Phoenix, Las Vegas, San Francisco, New Orleans, Houston, Chicago, Atlanta, New York (JFK), Washington) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Summer minimum temperature (°F) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Frequency / distribution of nights | Quantitative | Height/shape of filled density area (y-position/area) |
| Time period: 1960s | Temporal | Fill color (light gray) and direct label |
| Time period: 2020s | Temporal | Fill color (orange/pink shaded distribution) and direct label |
| Abnormally cold nights | Categorical/derived | Blue shaded tail area to the left of cold threshold; annotation text |
| Abnormally hot nights | Categorical/derived | Pink/red shaded tail area to the right of hot threshold; annotation text |
| Cold threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Hot threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Percent of nights abnormally cold | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |
| Percent of nights abnormally hot | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |

raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  "Is Global Warming that Big of a Deal? This Graph May Tell You!" by Samuel of Derby, Kansas; "It's Getting Hot and It Won't Stop" by Serena; “Climate Change, Nightly Warming” by Ronny of Perth Amboy High School in New Jersey; "The Quick and Steep Incline for Summer Temps" by Evan of New Hampshire, “Summer Sizzles” by Ashley of New York, “Hot Summer Nights” by Cierra, and "The Crazy Thing Climate Change Has Done To Our Summers” by Irina in Massachusetts, 
 
You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, May 6 to see the Reveal with the free link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.
 
Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  
 
Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, whose Mayor Wu released last week for Earth Day her plan to address Boston’s “heat islands,” which includes more trees, water bottle stations, green roofs and outdoor worker safety measures, and Annie Fetter near Philadelphia, who is grateful for the 200+ year old tree that shades her house.

- **Faceted density/distribution chart** (small multiples of overlaid smoothed distributions).
- Each panel shows temperature distributions for a city, with shaded regions highlighting unusually cold and unusually hot nights.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: separate panels for different cities.
- **Layering/overplotting**: multiple filled distribution shapes are overlaid within each panel.
- **Reference lines**: vertical dotted lines mark thresholds for abnormal cold/hot.
- **Text annotations**: percentages and labels are placed directly on panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City (Phoenix, Las Vegas, San Francisco, New Orleans, Houston, Chicago, Atlanta, New York (JFK), Washington) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Summer minimum temperature (°F) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Frequency / distribution of nights | Quantitative | Height/shape of filled density area (y-position/area) |
| Time period: 1960s | Temporal | Fill color (light gray) and direct label |
| Time period: 2020s | Temporal | Fill color (orange/pink shaded distribution) and direct label |
| Abnormally cold nights | Categorical/derived | Blue shaded tail area to the left of cold threshold; annotation text |
| Abnormally hot nights | Categorical/derived | Pink/red shaded tail area to the right of hot threshold; annotation text |
| Cold threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Hot threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Percent of nights abnormally cold | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |
| Percent of nights abnormally hot | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |

raw_comment:
Summer Sizzle 
      This graph shows how populated cities across the United States  temperature had differed over the last few decades through June and August.  Out of the 9 major cities surveyed New Orleans has the highest percentage of abnormally hot weather at 64% during those months . I am not surprised by the observation  because this state is furthest south out of every state surveyed. On average almost all of those states have gotten warmer throughout the decades besides Houston. I first wonder why these 9 states out of our whole country were surveyed. Is there a reason why these states in particular were surveyed?. I also wonder how New York has stayed so consistent in its temperatures over the decades compared to other states. This graph shows that the country has grown hotter over the decades and global warming is truly becoming an issue in our society. This graph shows the impact temperature has on our planet and how it's getting worse.

- **Faceted density/distribution chart** (small multiples of overlaid smoothed distributions).
- Each panel shows temperature distributions for a city, with shaded regions highlighting unusually cold and unusually hot nights.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: separate panels for different cities.
- **Layering/overplotting**: multiple filled distribution shapes are overlaid within each panel.
- **Reference lines**: vertical dotted lines mark thresholds for abnormal cold/hot.
- **Text annotations**: percentages and labels are placed directly on panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City (Phoenix, Las Vegas, San Francisco, New Orleans, Houston, Chicago, Atlanta, New York (JFK), Washington) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Summer minimum temperature (°F) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Frequency / distribution of nights | Quantitative | Height/shape of filled density area (y-position/area) |
| Time period: 1960s | Temporal | Fill color (light gray) and direct label |
| Time period: 2020s | Temporal | Fill color (orange/pink shaded distribution) and direct label |
| Abnormally cold nights | Categorical/derived | Blue shaded tail area to the left of cold threshold; annotation text |
| Abnormally hot nights | Categorical/derived | Pink/red shaded tail area to the right of hot threshold; annotation text |
| Cold threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Hot threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Percent of nights abnormally cold | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |
| Percent of nights abnormally hot | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted density/distribution chart** (small multiples of overlaid smoothed distributions).
- Each panel shows temperature distributions for a city, with shaded regions highlighting unusually cold and unusually hot nights.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: separate panels for different cities.
- **Layering/overplotting**: multiple filled distribution shapes are overlaid within each panel.
- **Reference lines**: vertical dotted lines mark thresholds for abnormal cold/hot.
- **Text annotations**: percentages and labels are placed directly on panels.

| Frequency / distribution of nights | Quantitative | Height/shape of filled density area (y-position/area) |
| Time period: 1960s | Temporal | Fill color (light gray) and direct label |
| Time period: 2020s | Temporal | Fill color (orange/pink shaded distribution) and direct label |
| Abnormally cold nights | Categorical/derived | Blue shaded tail area to the left of cold threshold; annotation text |
| Abnormally hot nights | Categorical/derived | Pink/red shaded tail area to the right of hot threshold; annotation text |
| Cold threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Hot threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |

raw_comment:
SUMMER SIZZLES

Summer nights are getting hotter, but from what I have observed there are barely any abnormally cold summers. Nearly 50% of the nights are actually abnormally hot. I wonder if global warming is the only cause for the increasing temperatures. I can relate to this because in my community we are very big on hanging out on summer nights and it’s hard to stay outside when it is very hot.

raw_comment:
Today’s graphs show the distributions of the daily summer minimum night temperatures in nine U.S. cities for the 1960s decade and the 2020s decade to date.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?”, “What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in these graphs. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the online article that included these graphs plus an interactive feature that animates for the seven decades since 1960 the distributions of temperatures for all cities with airports.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response (and replies made to it) to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, May 6 with moderation on Wednesday, May 11.  The topic – teen behaviors.  The May 11 graph will be the last “What’s Going On In This Graph?” for the school year.  Keep noticing and wondering.

4. "Summer Nights in the U.S.: 2020s Edition"

I notice that that only <1 - 3% of nights were abnormally cold, while in the 60s, it was much colder and the lowest temperatures were 5 - 20 degrees colder than they are as of 2020. The amount of abnormally high nights has also skyrocketed, likely because of global warming.

This is really a shock to me, because even though I knew that global warming is a big problem, I didn't know that it could completely change our average temperatures in only 60 years.

Don't think that global warming exists? Look at these graphs and think again!

- **Faceted density/distribution chart** (small multiples of overlaid smoothed distributions).
- Each panel shows temperature distributions for a city, with shaded regions highlighting unusually cold and unusually hot nights.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: separate panels for different cities.
- **Layering/overplotting**: multiple filled distribution shapes are overlaid within each panel.
- **Reference lines**: vertical dotted lines mark thresholds for abnormal cold/hot.
- **Text annotations**: percentages and labels are placed directly on panels.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that particularly in New York (JFK), the temperatures  had 3% abnormally cold nights and seems surprising when compared to the rest of the nine cities. This may be due to New York being located toward the Northeast coast when most of these other cities are located most toward the Western portion of the United States.

2. I wonder why there appears to be some sort of dip that occurs in San Francisco from 55 degrees to 60 degrees, as there appears to be nothing of the sort in other cities. I also wonder why in the majority of the nine cities (and especially Houston), it seems there is little to no change to summer night temperatures going from data collected in the 1960s to the 2020s. 

3. This relates to me and my community since it notifies us about what to expect in other states and reminds us to keep an eye on our own summer night temperatures. 

4. Title :  Temperature on a Rapid Rise in These Cities! Take a Look!

raw_comment:
1.   What do you notice?

   In terms of the graph, I notice that summer nights are increasingly hotter in the 2020s than they were in the 1960s, according to the nine graphs supplied. Additionally, New York (JFK) was the only city that had such a high abnormal cold (3% abnormally cold), which is in fact not even that cold. However, compared to the rest, it is the coldest. 

2.    What do you wonder?

   When it comes to the graph, I wonder what the orange sections on each of the graphs signify. I am also curious if location of the cities plays any part in the data collected in regards to abnormally hot and abnormally cold. Do states that are near one another display similar data, or are there underlying factors?

3.     How does this relate to you and your community?

   This relates to me and my community considering the fact that as summer is coming up, global warming is evident with the decrease in temperature that is currently going on. Thus, this graph relates to me as New Jersey is very close to New York, so it makes me question how this summer's temperatures will be, as well as if they will reflect the data on the graph. I can relate to the data from New York and also use the other cities to come to a conclusion about what is happening in my community, as well as the United States.   

4.     What’s going on in this graph?

   A catchy headline for this graph is: "Hot and Cold: Is Global Warming In Control?"

raw_comment:
Title Idea : The temperatures are rising, and not for a good reason.

I notice that all of the cities have been 17 % or more abnormally hot then what they were in the 1960s.  I have also noticed that the warmer cities (because of location) have increased the most in abnormal heat. I can see why they have increased the most, because they were already pretty hot to begin with, and because of global warming. I wonder why the colder cities haven't increased more than they have, because the warmer cities have also increased so much. Maybe its because  it depends on the population and density of the city.

## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted density/distribution chart** (small multiples of overlaid smoothed distributions).
- Each panel shows temperature distributions for a city, with shaded regions highlighting unusually cold and unusually hot nights.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: separate panels for different cities.
- **Layering/overplotting**: multiple filled distribution shapes are overlaid within each panel.
- **Reference lines**: vertical dotted lines mark thresholds for abnormal cold/hot.
- **Text annotations**: percentages and labels are placed directly on panels.

## 3. Data variables

|---|---|---|

| Summer minimum temperature (°F) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Frequency / distribution of nights | Quantitative | Height/shape of filled density area (y-position/area) |
| Time period: 1960s | Temporal | Fill color (light gray) and direct label |
| Time period: 2020s | Temporal | Fill color (orange/pink shaded distribution) and direct label |
| Abnormally cold nights | Categorical/derived | Blue shaded tail area to the left of cold threshold; annotation text |
| Abnormally hot nights | Categorical/derived | Pink/red shaded tail area to the right of hot threshold; annotation text |
| Cold threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Hot threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Percent of nights abnormally cold | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |
| Percent of nights abnormally hot | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |

- **Faceted density/distribution chart** (small multiples of overlaid smoothed distributions).
- Each panel shows temperature distributions for a city, with shaded regions highlighting unusually cold and unusually hot nights.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: separate panels for different cities.
- **Layering/overplotting**: multiple filled distribution shapes are overlaid within each panel.
- **Reference lines**: vertical dotted lines mark thresholds for abnormal cold/hot.
- **Text annotations**: percentages and labels are placed directly on panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City (Phoenix, Las Vegas, San Francisco, New Orleans, Houston, Chicago, Atlanta, New York (JFK), Washington) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Summer minimum temperature (°F) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Frequency / distribution of nights | Quantitative | Height/shape of filled density area (y-position/area) |
| Time period: 1960s | Temporal | Fill color (light gray) and direct label |
| Time period: 2020s | Temporal | Fill color (orange/pink shaded distribution) and direct label |
| Abnormally cold nights | Categorical/derived | Blue shaded tail area to the left of cold threshold; annotation text |
| Abnormally hot nights | Categorical/derived | Pink/red shaded tail area to the right of hot threshold; annotation text |
| Cold threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Hot threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Percent of nights abnormally cold | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |
| Percent of nights abnormally hot | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |

I wonder what the temperatures throughout the rest of the year look like, not just from June to August. I also wonder how temperatures might vary in other American cities and other locations around the world.

"The World is getting hotter"

1. I noticed that cities are getting hotter and hotter each decade. Also, a low amount of nights were abnormally cold, which indicates that also during the nights the temperatures are continuing to rise. 

2. I wonder how the temperature has rised this much over the years and if it is our fault. Also, I wonder the temperatures of the rest of the nights of the year and how much they differ from the temperatures of the other nights. 

3. These graphs relate to me and my community since global warming and climate change are topics that are thought a lot in schools recently. Also, it is mainly our fault if the temperatures are rising, and to try to avoid it we can stop polluting and throw away the trash in their appropiate garbage cans.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the graphs showed consistently higher night temperatures compared to those in the 1960s.

I wonder what caused New York's smaller rates of abnormal temperatures. I also wonder about the relationship between the population density/how that's changed since 1960 and the heat increase since 1960 because places with denser populations should have higher temperatures (body heat and released gases from carbon uses).

This relates to my community because, in just my lifetime alone, I have noticed an increase in heat every summer, shorter winters, and less consistent weather. This affects everywhere across the world, and third-world countries are getting the worst of it because they do not have the resources to create a more environmentally conscience environment and they are often home to factories supplying stores across the world. These factories release huge amounts of carbon, contributing to warmer temperatures and a less clean Earth. We should all make an active effort to reverse the effects of climate change, or at least prevent things from getting worse.

"It's Getting Hot and it Won't Stop"

- **Faceting / small multiples**: separate panels for different cities.

- **Reference lines**: vertical dotted lines mark thresholds for abnormal cold/hot.

sentence_classifications.image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted density/distribution chart** (small multiples of overlaid smoothed distributions).
- Each panel shows temperature distributions for a city, with shaded regions highlighting unusually cold and unusually hot nights.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: separate panels for different cities.
- **Layering/overplotting**: multiple filled distribution shapes are overlaid within each panel.
- **Reference lines**: vertical dotted lines mark thresholds for abnormal cold/hot.
- **Text annotations**: percentages and labels are placed directly on panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City (Phoenix, Las Vegas, San Francisco, New Orleans, Houston, Chicago, Atlanta, New York (JFK), Washington) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Summer minimum temperature (°F) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Frequency / distribution of nights | Quantitative | Height/shape of filled density area (y-position/area) |
| Time period: 1960s | Temporal | Fill color (light gray) and direct label |
| Time period: 2020s | Temporal | Fill color (orange/pink shaded distribution) and direct label |
| Abnormally cold nights | Categorical/derived | Blue shaded tail area to the left of cold threshold; annotation text |
| Abnormally hot nights | Categorical/derived | Pink/red shaded tail area to the right of hot threshold; annotation text |
| Cold threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Hot threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Percent of nights abnormally cold | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |
| Percent of nights abnormally hot | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |
